B0.p: A general heading for mythical animals, creatures that are not ordinary real animals.

B1.r: Irish myth: Cross.—N. A. Indian: *Alexander N. Am. 292 No. 40, ibid. 69 (Cherokee), 81 (Pawnee), 156 (Navaho).
B1.p: Animals have mythical elders, ancestral beings from which the animals of today are descended.

B1.1.p: Each kind of animal has a guardian angel in heaven.

B2.p: A group or family is linked to a particular animal that serves as its sacred emblem or protector.

B2.1.p: A dog is the totem animal of a people or family, its sacred emblem and protector.

B5.p: Fantastic creatures, birds and other imaginary beasts appear as subjects in works of art.

B7.p: Animals are placed in the sky or heavens, forming part of the celestial world.

B7.1.p: Animals are said to rule over the celestial spheres or heavenly realms.

B7.2.p: Mythical animals surround the throne of God in heaven.

B7.3.p: A mythical bird runs ahead of the sun and carries an inscription written in golden letters.

B10.p: Mythical beasts and creatures that are hybrids of different animals, or otherwise monstrous, are described.

B11.r: **Smith Dragon; *Fb Drager, lindorme, slanger i folkets tro (Særtryk af Naturen og Mennesket, 1894, pp. 164—196); *Nyrop Dania II 341ff.; *Róheim Drachen und Drachenkämpfer; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 364 ff.; Meyer Germanische Mythologie (1891) 95ff.; **Du Bose The Dragon, Image and Demon (London, 1886); Norlind Skattsägner 44f., 77f., Solheim Register 17; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 133ff., 176ff., (1928) 119ff.—*Type 300; *BP I 547.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 216; Celtic: *Henderson Celtic Dragon Myth (Edinburgh, 1911), *Cross; Lettish: Auning Ueber den lettischen Drachenmythus; Armenian: Ananikian 76ff; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Ferguson 101; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 169, No. 73.
B11.p: The dragon, a large winged serpent-like monster, is a mythical beast in folklore.

B11.1.p: Tales explain how a dragon comes into being or what its origin is.

B11.1.1.p: A dragon hatches from an egg laid by a cock, a rooster's egg.

B11.1.2.p: A white horse plunges into water and is transformed into a dragon.

B11.1.3.r: (Cf. B11.6.2.)—Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 367; Eisen Esthnische Mythologie 74ff.; Icel.: *Boberg.
B11.1.3.p: A man lying on his treasure is transformed into a dragon, as in the Fáfnir story.

B11.1.3.0.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; German: Grimm No. 88.
B11.1.3.0.1.p: A princess is transformed into a dragon.

B11.1.3.1.p: A dragon comes into being from a worm.

B11.1.3.1.1.r: De Vries Studien over Faerosche Balladen 122ff.; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 384f.; Icel.: *Boberg.
B11.1.3.1.1.p: A small worm placed on gold grows into a dragon, growing together with the gold it lies on.

B11.1.4.p: The devil takes the form of a dragon.

B11.2.p: Describes the physical form or appearance of a dragon.

B11.2.0.1.p: A dragon that is female, a she-dragon.

B11.2.1.r: (cf. B14.)—Smith Dragon 81 (serpent or crocodile, with scales of a fish for covering, and feet and wings and sometimes also the head, of an eagle, falcon, or hawk, and the forelimbs and sometimes the head of a lion).—Chinese: Werner 208 (ears of an ox, feet of a tiger, claws of an eagle, horns of a deer, head of a camel, eyes of a devil, neck of a snake, abdomen of a cock, scales of a carp); Egyptian: Smith op. cit. 79 (lioness, falcon, human being).
B11.2.1.p: A dragon built up from parts of several real animals, so it is a composite creature rather than a single kind of beast.

B11.2.1.1.r: Smith Dragon 92, 101f., 107ff. (American Indian, Japanese, East Indian).—Icel.: *Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 65.
B11.2.1.1.p: A dragon that is basically a snake but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.2.p: A dragon that is basically a lizard but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.3.r: Smith Dragon 108f.; Irish myth: Cross; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 65.
B11.2.1.3.p: A dragon that is basically a fish but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.4.p: A dragon that is basically a shellfish but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.5.p: A dragon that is basically a toad but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.6.p: A dragon that is basically an elephant but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.7.p: A dragon that is basically a horse but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.9.r: Smith Dragon 134 (Egyptian, Soudanese, West African, Hindu, Chinese, Japanese, American Indian). The evidence of this identification is merely the spiral horn.
B11.2.1.9.p: A dragon that is basically a ram, a male sheep, but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.10.p: A dragon that is basically a deer but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.11.p: A dragon that is basically an eagle but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.1.12.p: A dragon that is basically some other animal, not listed separately, but with altered features added to it.

B11.2.2.r: Smith Dragon 108 (blue), 137 (red).—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “dragons” (regiment of green dragons).—Icel.: Bósa saga 62 (golden).
B11.2.2.p: The colour of a dragon's body or features.

B11.2.2.1.p: A dragon whose feathers are gold.

B11.2.3.r: (Cf. B15.1.2.)—Danish: Fb “hoved” 65b; Jones PMLA XXIII 569.—Greek: Fox 87 (hundred); Persian: Carnoy 265 (three); Japanese: Anesaki 228 (eight), 333 (nine).

B11.2.3.1.r: *Type 300; Smith Dragon 211f.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bête”. Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 42 No. 302*A: Gaster Thespis 80f, 186.—India: Thompson-Balys; Araucanian: Alexander Lat. Am. 327.

B11.2.3.2.r: Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Africa (Fulah): Frobenius Atlantis VI 182ff. No. 4.

B11.2.3.5.p: A dragon that has twelve heads.

B11.2.3.6.p: A dragon that has two heads.

B11.2.4.p: A dragon's feet are described or have some notable feature.

B11.2.4.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Japanese: Smith Dragon 101f.; Chinese: Werner 368.
B11.2.4.1.p: A dragon's feet are notable for their number, such as having an unusual count of them.

B11.2.4.2.r: Cloven hoofs: Smith Dragon 137.—Claws: Chinese: Werner 368.
B11.2.4.2.p: A dragon's feet are notable for what they are made of or what they are like in nature.

B11.2.5.r: Smith Dragon 137.—Chinese: Werner 368, Eberhard FFC CXX 73, 85.
B11.2.5.p: A dragon has horns on its head.

B11.2.6.p: A dragon has wings, which are described in the tale.

B11.2.7.p: Snakes grow out of a dragon's shoulders.

B11.2.8.r: Smith Dragon 137; Fb “drage” (if one throws fire over dragon’s long tail, the tail falls and is full of treasure).
B11.2.8.p: A dragon has a tail, which is described in the tale.

B11.2.8.1.p: A dragon wraps its tail around a city so that the whole city is encircled.

B11.2.9.p: A dragon has a heart with some notable property, such as being the key to its life or power.

B11.2.10.p: A dragon's body is covered in scales.

B11.2.11.r: *Type 300; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 391; Fb. “drage”, “gloende” (glowing eyes and tongue), “ild” (fire from mouth). Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: *Boberg.

B11.2.11.2.r: Scotland, England: *Baughman Chinese: Werner 236.—N. A. Indian (Iroquois): BBAE XXX pt. 2, 720 s.v. “Teharonhiawagon”.
B11.2.11.2.p: A dragon's breath is so deadly that it kills a man.

B11.2.12.r: Jewish: Bin Gorion Born Judas II 170, 349, Neuman; Irish myth: Cross; African (Fang): Einstein 47.
B11.2.12.p: A dragon is of enormous size.

B11.2.13.p: A dragon has blood with some notable property.

B11.2.14.p: A dragon has a jewel set in its head.

B11.3.p: Where dragons live, the places they make their home.

B11.3.1.r: Smith Dragon 82.—Chinese: Werner 210 (only in autumn and winter); Icel.: Boberg.
B11.3.1.p: A dragon lives at the bottom of the sea.

B11.3.1.1.p: A dragon lives in a lake.

B11.3.1.2.p: A dragon's home is hidden beneath a waterfall.

B11.3.2.p: A dragon lives at the top of a mountain, and its breath forms clouds that hide the peak.

B11.3.3.r: Chinese: Werner 210 (only in spring and summer). (Cf. B11.4.1.)
B11.3.3.p: A dragon pays a visit to the sky, where it goes to live or travel above the earth.

B11.3.4.r: Mediaeval Romance: Wells Manual of Writings 39 (Nennius’s Historia Britonum) 42f. (Arthour and Merlin).

B11.3.5.r: (Cf. A1070.)—Zingerle Zs. f. deutsche Mythologie und Sittengeschichte II 347; Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 890.—Irish myth: Cross.
B11.3.5.p: A dragon lives underground, and its movements shake loose buildings or whole villages above.

B11.3.6.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319, 352.

B11.3.7.r: Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 179ff., (1928) 122ff.—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319.
B11.3.7.p: A dragon lives beneath a tree.

B11.3.8.p: A dragon lives on a remote, isolated island.

B11.4.p: Habits and behaviour typical of dragons.

B11.4.1.r: (cf. B11.2.1.11.)—BP III 423; *Fb “drage” (flies over the mountain).—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 319, 345; *Boberg; Greek myth: *Frazer Apollodorus I 38 n. 2 (air-going chariot and dragons); Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
B11.4.1.p: A dragon that can fly through the air.

B11.4.2.p: A dragon that gives signs or warnings of future events.

B11.4.4.p: A dragon that travels across either the sea or the land.

B11.5.1.p: A dragon that can change its shape at will.

B11.5.2.p: A dragon that can make itself magically invisible.

B11.5.3.r: Can see a fly miles away.—Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 97 No. 18.
B11.5.3.p: A dragon with miraculous or supernatural powers of sight.

B11.5.4.r: Gold Coast: Barker and Sinclair 97 No. 18.
B11.5.4.p: A dragon moves with incredible, almost magical speed.

B11.5.5.r: (cf. B11.2.3, B11.11.2.)—*Type 300; BP I 547; Eng.: Baughman; Greek: Fox 81 (hydra).—Onondaga: Beauchamp JAFL II 261.
B11.5.5.p: A dragon's severed head grows back on its own or returns to its body by itself.

B11.6.p: Dragons are shown doing various kinds of deeds, such as guarding things, helping people, or harming them.

B11.6.1.p: A dragon helps a hero because the hero once did it a kindness.

B11.6.1.2.p: A grateful dragon saves a hero and also frees him from prison.

B11.6.2.r: *Norlind Skattsägner 77f.; Gould Scandinavian Studies and Notes IX (1917) 170 No. 4; Penzer III 133; Smith Dragon 157—165; Finnish-Swedish; Wessman 76, 78 Nos. 632, 657; Icel.: Boberg; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 133ff., (1928) 119ff., III (1895) 454ff., (1931) 311ff.; Greek: *Grote I 219; U.S.: Baughman; Wienert FFC LVI 37; Phaedrus IV 21; Chinese: Werner 209.
B11.6.2.p: A dragon guards a hoard of treasure.

B11.6.2.1.p: A dragon guarding treasure has to surrender it when steel is thrown at it.

B11.6.2.2.p: Serpents are shown playing with a precious green stone.

B11.6.2.3.p: A dragon's pearl is stolen from it.

B11.6.3.p: A dragon eats treasure as its food.

B11.6.4.p: A dragon protects a holy land.

B11.6.5.p: A dragon guards a hermit's food and scares off robbers who try to take it.

B11.6.6.p: A dragon guards a bridge that leads to the otherworld.

B11.6.7.p: A dragon eats an ox at every meal.

B11.6.8.p: A dragon flies to its nest carrying a human being.

B11.6.8.1.p: A dragon flies away carrying off a lion.

B11.6.9.p: A dragon gnaws at the roots of a tree.

B11.6.10.p: A dragon with poisonous breath guards a sandalwood tree.

B11.7.p: A dragon acts as a spirit that controls rain.

B11.7.1.p: A dragon controls the water supply.

B11.7.1.1.p: A dragon is responsible for causing a flood, because it controls the water supply.

B11.7.2.r: Penzer VII 235 N. 2; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
B11.7.2.p: A dragon guards a lake, keeping control over the water it holds.

B11.8.r: Smith Dragon 82, 97.—Chinese: Werner 208ff., Graham. Icel.: Boberg.
B11.8.p: A dragon acts as a force for good, helping people rather than harming them.

B11.9.r: Smith Dragon 82.—Irish myth; Chinese: Werner 208 (introduced by the Buddhists).
B11.9.p: A dragon acts as a force of evil, harming people. The note adds that dragons are usually seen this way everywhere except in the East, where beneficent dragons are also found.

B11.10.r: *Type 300; Penzer VII 236, 240; Dickson Valentine and Orson 226f.; Gaster Thespis 176; Hartland Legend of Perseus passim; Fb “drage”, “pige”.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 34; Persian: Carnoy 320; India: *Thompson-Balys; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “exposition”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXXIX 17; Missouri French: Carrière; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 41; Japanese: Anesaki 249.
B11.10.p: A human being is sacrificed to a dragon, offered to it as food or to appease it.

B11.10.0.1.p: Animals, rather than a human being, are sacrificed to a dragon.

B11.10.1.p: A dragon keeps a maiden tied up with a golden chain, holding her captive.

B11.10.2.p: A dragon demands people as payment or tribute, and eats them as its rent.

B11.11.r: *Type 300; *BP I 547; *Smith Dragon 79ff., 104; *Róheim Drachen und Drachenkämpfer; *Norlind Skattsägner 67f., *Liebrecht Zur Volkskunde 70; **von Sydow Sigurds Strid med Fåvne; *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt I 204 nn. 1, 2; Clouston Pop. München 1914); *Loomis White Magic 65, 119; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus 27 no. 4 (Apollo and Python), I 153 n. 1 (Bellerophon and Chimera); Celtic: MacCulloch Celtic 130ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman, Gaster Thespis 140 ff., 326ff.; Egyptian: Müller 127; Persian: Carnoy 266, 270, 273, 322, *325, 329f.; Hindu: Keith 33 (Indra); India: *Thompson-Balys; Armenian: Ananikian 77; Japanese: Anesaki 228; Chinese: Werner 224, 361, Eberhard FFC CXX 105, 138; Arabian: Burton I 172.—English: Wells Manual of Writings 16 (Guy of Warwick), 115 (Sir Eglamour), 117 (Torrent of Portyngale); Missouri French: Carrière; Africa (Fang): Einstein 44, 47.—Cf. *Olrik Ragnarök 57ff. (fight with giant serpent).
B11.11.p: A hero or other character fights a dragon. It is a standard episode of dragon-slaying stories.

B11.11.1.r: French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXXIX 21; Missouri French: Carrière.
B11.11.1.p: In a fight with a dragon, the hero is given a respite, but the dragon returns stronger than before.

B11.11.2.p: The hero's dogs, or horse, keep the cut-off heads of the dragon from rejoining its body.

B11.11.3.p: When attacked, the dragon defends itself by shooting showers of fiery spines.

B11.11.4.r: Icel.: *Boberg. (See also R111.1. and most of the references to B11.11.).
B11.11.4.p: A hero fights a dragon in order to free a princess.

B11.11.5.p: A hero fights a dragon in order to free a man.

B11.11.6.p: A hero fights a dragon in order to free a lion.

B11.11.8.p: After men rebel against a dragon's demands, the dragon doubles what it asks for.

B11.12.p: Other characteristics of dragons that do not fit the categories above.

B11.12.1.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 171 No. 136; Irish myth: Cross; Eng.: Baughman; Gaster Oldest Stories 69.
B11.12.1.p: A dragon cannot be killed with ordinary weapons.

B11.12.1.1.p: A dragon that cannot be harmed by weapons is defeated by a kick to its vulnerable spot.

B11.12.1.2.p: A dragon that cannot be killed by weapons is wounded, but it dips the injured part into a holy well and is healed at once.

B11.12.2.p: A dragon's shriek makes the land around it barren and unable to grow anything.

B11.12.3.p: The dragon is a fiery creature that breathes or is made of fire.

B11.12.4.p: The dragon is fond of milk and will be drawn to or pacified by it.

B11.12.4.1.p: To keep a dragon calm, people feed it large amounts of milk.

B11.12.5.p: A dragon who rules over other dragons or serpents as their king.

B11.12.6.p: A dragon can hear a child crying even from a very great distance away.

B11.12.7.p: A human and a dragon marry each other.

B12.r: *Polívka Zs. f. Vksk. XXVII 46ff.; *Fb “basilisk”; *A Guichot y Sierra El Basilisco (Folklore Español III 9—83); *Norlind Skattsägner 46 n. 1; Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Basilisk”; Köhler-Bolte I 133.—English: Wells Manual of Writings 105 (Prose Alexander); Jewish: Neuman.
B12.p: A basilisk is a mythical lizard or serpent whose hissing drives other serpents away.

B12.1.r: Usually, a seven-year-old cock. Egg must lie in manure. (Cf. B11.1.1.)—*Polívka Zs. f. Vksk. XXVIII 46ff.; *Fb. “basilisk” I 53a, IV 29a; De Vries Het Sprookje 19—97; Taylor PMLA XXXVI 35ff.; Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Basilisk”.
B12.1.p: A basilisk is born from an egg laid by a rooster (cock).

B12.2.r: *Fb “basilisk” I 53a, IV 29a, “øje” III 1167b; Penzer VIII 75 n.l.
B12.2.p: A basilisk's gaze can paralyze or kill anyone who looks into its eyes.

B12.3.r: *Fb “basilisk” I 53a, “spejl” III 48a; Ward Catalogue of Romances III 194; Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 139; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 935.
B12.3.p: A basilisk, a deadly serpent-like monster, dies when it sees its own reflection or image.

B13.r: (cf. B15.7.2.)—*Type 1640; *BP I 164; **Odell Shepard The Lore of the Unicorn (London, 1929); **Robert Brown Jr. The Unicorn, a Mythological Investigation (London, 1881); Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 232f.; Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Einhorn”; Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 212; Icel.: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Ferguson 98.
B13.p: A unicorn, a one-horned horse-like creature.

B14.p: Mythical animals that are combinations of two or more different kinds of animal.

B14.1.r: Combination of lion, dragon, and goat. Breathes fire.—*Frazer Apollodorus I 151 n. 2, 153 n. 1; Fox 39.—Egyptian: Müller 169.
B14.1.p: A chimera, a monster made of parts of several different animals, typically lion, goat and serpent.

B14.2.p: An animal with the body of a horse and the legs of a hound (dog).

B14.3.r: S. A. Indian (Araucanìan): Cooper BBAE CXLIII II 753.
B14.3.p: A monstrous hybrid that is part calf and part sheep.

B15.p: Animals whose limbs or body parts are unusual in shape or number.

B15.1.p: An animal whose head is unusual in some way.

B15.1.1.p: Animals that have no head at all.

B15.1.1.1.p: A dog that has no head.

B15.1.2.r: (Cf. B15.7.2.)—Irish myth: Cross; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 357 n. 287f.—Africa (Angola): Chatelain 93 No. 5.
B15.1.2.p: A mythical animal that has many heads.

B15.1.2.1.p: A mythical animal that has two heads.

B15.1.2.1.1.p: A serpent with a head at each end of its body, one in front and one at the rear.

B15.1.2.1.2.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 142—158 passim.

B15.1.2.1.3.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 155.

B15.1.2.2.p: A mythical animal that has three heads.

B15.1.2.3.p: A mythical animal that has four heads.

B15.1.2.4.p: A mythical animal that has five heads.

B15.1.2.5.p: A mythical animal that has six heads.

B15.1.2.6.p: A mythical animal that has seven heads.

B15.1.2.6.1.r: Gaster Thespis 80f.; Hindu: Keith 154; Zanzibar: Bateman 134.

B15.1.2.7.p: A mythical animal that has eight heads.

B15.1.2.8.p: A mythical animal that has nine heads.

B15.1.2.8.1.p: A nine-headed monster called the hydra, whose middle head cannot die.

B15.1.2.10.p: A mythical animal with many heads, in forms other than those already listed in this group.

B15.1.2.10.2.p: A giant serpent monster with a hundred heads.

B15.1.2.10.3.p: A giant serpent with a thousand heads.

B15.1.3.p: An animal whose head is made of bone.

B15.2.p: A mythical animal with many mouths.

B15.3.p: An animal that is unusual in the number or form of its horns.

B15.3.0.2.p: An ox with only one horn.

B15.3.2.p: An animal with a horn of gold or of silver.

B15.3.2.1.p: A deer with one gold horn and one silver horn.

B15.3.2.2.p: A goat with one gold horn and one silver horn.

B15.3.2.3.p: An ox whose horns are made of gold.

B15.3.2.3.1.p: A cow whose horns are silver, one of the golden-horned ox type of animal with precious metal horns.

B15.3.3.p: A deer that has an enormous antler, far larger than a normal deer's.

B15.3.4.p: A normally harmless animal that has grown horns, which makes it an unusual, marvelous creature.

B15.3.4.1.p: A hare that has horns on its head.

B15.3.4.2.r: S. A Indian (Chaco): Belaieff BBAE CXLIII (1) 379.
B15.3.4.2.p: A horned armadillo that lives underground.

B15.3.5.p: An animal with a single horn on its head that points upward toward the sky.

B15.4.p: Animals that have unusual eyes, differing in number, appearance or effect from ordinary eyes.

B15.4.1.1.r: Southern Ute: Lowie JAFL XXXVII 49 No. 24.

B15.4.1.2.r: S. A. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 144.

B15.4.1.3.r: S. A. Indian (Yuracare): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 503.

B15.4.2.p: Beasts whose eyes burn with fire.

B15.4.2.1.p: A dog whose eyes contain fire, so they blaze and glow.

B15.4.3.p: Dogs whose eyes are as large and round as plates or teacups.

B15.4.4.p: An animal that has human eyes, because it is a man transformed into an animal.

B15.4.5.p: A pig that has only one eye.

B15.5.p: Animals that have an unusual nose or snout, differing from ordinary ones.

B15.5.1.p: A horse whose nostrils breathe out fire.

B15.5.2.p: An animal with a snout made of iron.

B15.6.p: Animals that have unusual legs or feet, differing from the normal number or form of an animal's limbs.

B15.6.0.1.p: An animal that has only one foot.

B15.6.1.r: Fb. “trebenet”; Zingerle Sagen aus Tirol 590; Tobler Epiphanie der Seele 20; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 420. Mannhardt Germanische Mythen 409; Wehrhan Freimauerei 53 (hare).—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 152.
B15.6.1.p: A four-footed animal that has only three legs.

B15.6.2.p: Empousa, a monster with one foot of brass and the other of an ass.

B15.6.3.r: Ipolyi Zs. f. deutsche Mythologie II 269.—Hindu: Penzer III 259 n. 1 (sarabhas); Irish myth: Cross.
B15.6.3.p: Animals that have many more legs than is normal.

B15.6.3.1.p: A four-footed animal with six legs.

B15.6.4.p: A bull that has human hands and feet instead of hooves or paws.

B15.7.r: (Cf. B20, B142, B92.) Irish myth: Cross.
B15.7.p: Other mythical animals with unusual limbs or body parts not covered by the preceding groups.

B15.7.1.p: Cerberus, the hell hound with three heads, a serpent's tail, and a writhing mass of snakes sprouting from its body.

B15.7.2.r: Stands in the ocean. Has three feet, six eyes, nine mouths, two ears, one horn, a white body. Two eyes are in eye position, two on top of his head, two on his hump. He renders powerless by the sharpness of his eyes. He has three mouths in his head, three in his hump, and three in the inner parts of his flanks. Each mouth is the size of a cottage. (Cf. B13, B15.1, B15.2, B15.4.)—Persian: Carnoy 270.
B15.7.2.p: A monstrous ass with three legs.

B15.7.3.p: A bird whose head is gold and whose wings are silver.

B15.7.4.p: A fox with a tail forked into eight parts.

B15.7.5.p: The Ghormuhas, monsters with men's bodies, horses' heads, one leg, and who eat human flesh.

B15.7.7.1.r: Korean: Zong-in-Sob 230 No. 99, 20 No. 9, 38 No. 22; Japanese: Ikeda; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 141.

B15.7.8.p: A boar with nine tusks in each jaw.

B15.7.9.p: A cow whose liver is made of tallow (hard animal fat) instead of ordinary flesh.

B15.7.9.1.p: A cow carries two bags inside it: one holds a bird with one leg, the other holds a bird with twelve legs.

B15.7.10.p: An animal whose skin is unusual or strange in some way.

B15.7.10.1.p: An animal whose skin is horny, like hard horn or thick plates.

B15.7.10.2.p: An animal whose hair is made of iron pins or needles.

B15.7.11.p: A single-headed animal with two bodies and six legs.

B15.7.12.p: An eel with a mane of fire.

B15.7.13.p: A bird whose beak is on fire.

B15.7.13.1.p: A bird whose beak is made of iron.

B15.7.14.p: A bird whose tail is made of fire.

B15.7.15.p: A monster with a hundred hands, each hand having a hundred palms and each palm a hundred nails.

B15.7.16.p: A mythical eagle has twelve wings and three heads.

B16.p: Mythical animals that cause great destruction to people, crops or property.

B16.0.1.p: Beasts that wreck vineyards and steal the fruit.

B16.0.2.p: A tormenting beast lives inside a man's stomach and causes him torment.

B16.0.3.p: A man-eating monster that lives in a cave.

B16.1.p: Ordinary farm or household animals that have become destructive monsters.

B16.1.1.r: Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 191; Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chat”; India: Thompson-Balys.
B16.1.1.p: A monstrous cat that lays waste to a whole country.

B16.1.1.1.p: A monstrous cat that is born of a pig.

B16.1.1.2.p: A cat leaps through a man like a fiery arrow and reduces him to ashes.

B16.1.1.3.p: A cat devours the flesh of a man's legs.

B16.1.2.p: A dog that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.1.2.1.p: A dog of enormous size that acts as a destructive monster.

B16.1.3.p: A horse that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.1.4.p: A pig or hog that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.1.4.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: *Boberg; Greek: Fox 82; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 2; India: Thompson-Balys.
B16.1.4.1.p: A boar of enormous size that acts as a destructive monster.

B16.1.4.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: MacCulloch Celtic 187, *Fb “sø” III 450a.
B16.1.4.2.p: A sow of enormous size that acts as a destructive monster.

B16.1.5.p: Cattle that are destructive monsters and kill or devour people.

B16.1.5.1.r: Babylonian: Jensen Gilgamesch-Epos VI 94ff., cf. 120—21, 129ff.; Greek: Fox 29, 62, 84, 102; Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 85, *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
B16.1.5.1.p: A monstrous ox or bull is killed.

B16.1.5.2.p: A cow that is destructive because it is possessed by demons.

B16.1.5.3.p: A bull that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.1.6.p: A sheep that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.1.6.1.p: A lamb with supernatural powers that causes great destruction.

B16.2.p: Wild animals that are destructive monsters, ravaging people and property.

B16.2.1.p: A fox that is a destructive monster, which demands a human sacrifice every month.

B16.2.2.p: A tiger that is a destructive monster, ravaging people and property.

B16.2.3.r: Babylonian: Jensen Gilgamesch-Epos VIII; Greek: Fox 80; Icel.: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
B16.2.3.p: A giant lion that is a destructive monster is defeated by a hero.

B16.2.4.p: A giant wolf that is a destructive monster is defeated by a hero.

B16.2.5.p: A bear that is a destructive monster is killed.

B16.2.6.r: Icel.: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese-Persian: Coyajee JPASB XXIV 188.
B16.2.6.p: A mythical elephant that causes great destruction, wrecking or killing people and property.

B16.2.7.p: A deer that causes great destruction, wrecking land or harming people.

B16.2.8.p: Enormous mice that attack and eat people.

B16.2.9.p: A bison or buffalo that causes great destruction.

B16.3.p: Wild birds that cause great destruction, harming people, animals, or land.

B16.4.p: A giant fish that devastates the area by carrying off one victim every day.

B16.4.1.p: A sea monster called a leviathan throws up a gorge or chasm that spreads sickness across the land.

B16.4.1.1.p: A leviathan strikes the earth with its tail, causing a huge catastrophe.

B16.4.1.1.2.p: A sea beast whose breath or belching spreads disease on land, kills birds when it rises upward, and kills fish and sea creatures when it sinks downward.

B16.5.p: Giant reptiles that cause great destruction, harming people and land.

B16.5.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 144f.—Africa (Chaga): Stamberg Zs. f. Eingeborenen-Spr. XXIII 296ff., Gutmann Volksbuch der Wadschagga 82f. No. 41, (Ganda): Baskerville King of the Snakes 1ff., (Senegambia): Béranger-Feraud Recueil de Contes Populaires de la Senegambia II 185ff. No. 2, (tribes of Western Sudan): Tauxier Le Noir du Yatengo 496 No. 1.
B16.5.1.p: A giant serpent that causes great destruction.

B16.5.1.1.p: A destructive serpent that breathes fire.

B16.5.1.2.p: A man-eating sea monster in the form of a serpent that causes great destruction.

B16.5.1.2.1.p: A serpent sucks the breath or blood out of a man.

B16.5.2.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX II No. 188.
B16.5.2.p: A destructive crocodile that harms people and land.

B16.5.3.p: A destructive shellfish that causes great harm.

B16.5.4.p: A giant turtle that eats people.

B16.6.p: Insects that cause great destruction, harming people and land.

B16.6.1.p: Giant ants that attack and eat people.

B16.6.2.p: A beetle of the chafer kind that sucks blood, causing great harm.

B16.6.2.1.p: A fierce black chafer (a beetle) is a devastating mythical insect that sucks blood, one of the insects that attack and destroy people and property.

B16.6.3.p: Locusts with iron wings swarm in and eat up the wheat crop, destroying the harvest.

B16.6.4.p: A giant spider that causes great destruction, ravaging people or property.

B16.6.5.p: A giant centipede that causes great destruction.

B17.p: Mythical animals that are hostile and attack people rather than helping them.

B17.1.p: Hostile beasts: wild or monstrous animals that set upon people.

B17.1.1.p: Ferocious animals are set loose on those who attack or pursue someone, so the beasts act as guardians.

B17.1.2.p: A hostile dog or hound that attacks people, often as a monster.

B17.1.2.1.p: Bloodhounds attack a victim and cut off his head.

B17.1.2.2.p: A hostile hound is killed when a person reaches through a hollow log, grabs its jaws, and tears out its heart.

B17.1.2.2.1.p: A hero kills a hostile hound monster by tearing out its entrails or heart.

B17.1.2.3.p: A man who has been transformed into a hostile dog attacks people.

B17.1.3.p: Cattle that are hostile and attack people.

B17.1.4.p: A hostile horse that attacks people.

B17.1.4.1.p: Horses in a rage attack and kill their driver.

B17.1.5.p: A hostile cat that attacks people.

B17.2.p: Other hostile animals that attack people, not covered by the beast or domestic-animal categories.

B17.2.1.p: Hostile sea creatures that attack people at sea or on the shore.

B17.2.1.1.p: A hostile sea-rat that attacks people.

B17.2.1.2.p: A hostile eel attacks the hero.

B17.2.1.3.p: A sea-cat is a mythical sea creature that attacks people and is hostile to them.

B17.2.2.p: A griffin, a mythical winged beast, is hostile and attacks people.

B17.2.3.p: A raven is hostile and attacks people.

B17.2.3.1.p: A raven attacks people by pulling out their eyes.

B17.2.4.p: A scorpion is hostile and attacks people.

B17.2.4.1.p: A scorpion attacks people by scooping out their eyes.

B18.p: A behemoth is a mythical animal of huge size.

B19.p: A miscellaneous category of other mythical beasts that do not fit the groups above.

B19.1.r: (Cf. B15.6, B15.5)—Frazer Apollodorus I 109 n. 4, 110 n. i.
B19.1.p: Bulls with feet of bronze that breathe fire.

B19.2.p: A magical cow that gives nectar, a sweet divine drink, instead of milk.

B19.2.1.p: The cow Audhumla, a primeval cow of Norse myth whose milk nourishes the first beings.

B19.3.p: A horse hatches from an egg. A mythical hero will later come riding on such a horse.

B19.3.2.r: S. A. Indian: Toba Métraux MAFLS XL 50.
B19.3.2.p: A mythical horse owned by a water-spirit.

B19.4.r: (Cf. B15.4.2.)—*Wuttke Der deutsche Volksaberglaube der Gegenwart 59; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “glühend”; *Fb “gloende”.—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Icel.: Boberg.
B19.4.p: Animals, such as horses or swine, that glow.

B19.4.1.p: Swine that burrow into the ground and make it hot.

B19.4.2.p: A serpent that is fiery or glowing with fire.

B19.4.3.p: A sheep wearing a collar of fire.

B19.4.4.p: A hound that is a flame of fire by night.

B19.5.p: A horse with a mane of gold.

B19.6.p: A herd of animals that is said to have come down from heaven, a marvelous divine herd of beasts.

B19.6.1.p: Cattle belonging to the sun, a mythical herd that is part of the heavenly herd motif.

B19.7.p: Heidrun, a mythical goat that feeds on the leaves of a tree and provides mead or milk.

B19.8.p: A mythical antelope, an imaginary beast of the antelope kind.

B19.9.r: S. A. Indian (Guarani): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 93.
B19.9.p: Bats that live forever, immortal bats in a mythical setting.

B19.10.p: A mythical tiger, an imaginary or magical tiger.

B19.11.p: A mythical donkey, an imaginary or magical ass.

B20.p: Beast-men, creatures that combine animal and human form.

B20.1.p: An army made up of creatures that are half animal and half man.

B20.2.p: Beast-men who live in the lower world, the underworld.

B21.r: **P. V. C. Baur Centaurs in Ancient Art (Berlin, 1912); *Frazer Apollodorus I 191 n. 3, 261 n. 1; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 413; Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 225ff.; **Dumézil (G.) Le Probleme des Centaures (Paris, 1929); Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Penzer I 202.
B21.p: A centaur, a creature with the trunk and head of a man and the body of a horse.

B21.1.p: The Norse man-horse, a centaur-like creature called fingalkn or fingalp in Norse lore.

B21.2.p: A creature with a human body and hands but the head and ears of a horse.

B21.3.p: A man who has a horse's mouth.

B22.r: *Chauvin VII 82 No. 373bis, n. I; Jewish: Neuman.
B22.p: A man-ass, a creature with a human body and the hooves of a donkey.

B22.1.p: A creature with a human body and the head of a donkey.

B22.2.p: A donkey that has human intelligence and can think and speak like a person.

B23.p: A man-bull, a creature that is part man and part bull.

B23.1.r: Icel.: Boberg; Greek: Fox 61; Roscher Lexikon s. v. “Acheloos”; Frazer Apollodorus I 307 n. I, II 120 n. I.—Chauvin VII 87 No. 373bis n. 3.—Chinese: Ferguson 30.
B23.1.p: The Minotaur, a creature with a man's body and a bull's head, born of a woman who united with a bull.

B23.2.p: A bull that has a man's head.

B23.3.p: A man who has two horns growing on his head, marking him as part human and part bull.

B24.r: Combination of man and goat.—Greek: Fox 268; Jewish: Neuman.
B24.p: A satyr: a mythical creature with the body of a man and features of a goat.

B24.1.p: A satyr discloses to a husband that his wife has been unfaithful.

B24.2.p: A man whose head is that of a goat.

B25.r: Icel.: *Boberg; American Indian and Siberian: *Jochelson JE VI, 1912, 336; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 205, III 226, 246, Holm 50, Rink 47, 111, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 633; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 205.
B25.p: A creature with the body of a man and the head or features of a dog.

B25.1.r: *Chauvin VII 77 No. 121; H. Cordier RTP V 72ff.; Fb “hundetyrk”.—Loomis White Magic 114; Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 72.
B25.1.p: A man whose head is that of a dog.

B25.1.1.p: A dog-headed man who has the mane of a horse or of cattle.

B25.1.2.r: Estonian: M. J. Eisen Estnische Mythologie (Leipzig 1925) pp. 202—206; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 73 No. 232; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3911.
B25.1.2.p: A people who are dog-headed; peasants are persecuted by one-eyed and dog-headed savages.

B25.2.p: A dog whose head is that of a human being.

B26.p: A creature with the body of a man and features of a tiger.

B26.1.p: A girl who has a tiger's legs and ears.

B27.r: Greek: *Grote I 7; Jewish: Neuman; Chauvin VII 87 No. 373bis n. 3.
B27.p: A creature with a man's body and a lion's head.

B28.p: A creature with a man's body and an elephant's head.

B29.p: Mythical hybrids of animal and human that do not fit the other beast-man types.

B29.1.r: *Bolte FFC XXXIX 5 n. 1—Icel.: Herrmann Saxo II 603; Czech: Máchal Slavic 265; India: Thompson-Balys.
B29.1.p: A monster with a woman's face and a serpent's body, or a sow's body with horse's legs.

B29.2.p: A monster that is half woman and half serpent.

B29.2.1.p: A serpent that has a human head.

B29.2.2.p: A man whose head is that of a serpent.

B29.2.3.p: A snake-bodied creature with the head of a woman.

B29.3.p: A creature that is part man and part hog or pig.

B29.4.p: A being that is part man and part cat.

B29.4.1.p: A man-cat whose head is a cat's head.

B29.4.1.1.p: A man who has a cat's head and also a cat's tail.

B29.5.p: A being that is part man and part wolf.

B29.6.p: A being that is part man and part elk.

B29.7.p: A being that is part man and part bear.

B29.8.p: A being whose upper body is like a hedgehog's, with the rest human.

B29.9.p: A being that is part man and part ape.

B30.r: Penzer VII 56 n.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 29.
B30.p: A general heading for mythical birds, which are imaginary birds of folk belief.

B30.2.p: A mythical cock, a rooster of folk belief with supernatural qualities.

B31.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; German: Grimm Nos. 51, 161; Penzer I 103ff., II 219; Chauvin VI 3 No. 181 n. 3; Burton I 154 n., V 122f., VI 16n, 48ff., S III 186, S VII 249.—Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 45.—N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 318 n. 151.
B31.1.p: The roc, a giant bird that carries off men in its claws.

B31.1.0.1.p: Ziz, a giant bird in Hebrew tradition that corresponds to the roc.

B31.1.1.p: The roc's egg, which is found or taken in some tale.

B31.1.2.p: A roc drops a rock so large that it destroys a ship.

B31.2.r: Fb “Fugl Gam”, “Gam” IV 173b.—Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 131ff., (1928) 94.—Icel.: *Boberg.
B31.2.p: The bird Gam, which throws sand into a stream to make a lake, carries men, and leaps into the sea to sleep.

B31.3.p: Giant ravens that sit on a mountain and cause an avalanche when they fly off.

B31.3.1.p: A giant raven that can swim.

B31.4.p: A giant bat, an enormous bat of folk fancy.

B31.5.p: The simorg, a giant bird of Persian legend.

B31.6.r: Penzer I 104, VI 123 n.—Chinese: Giles Strange Stories of a Chinese Studio (New York, 1927) 547.—Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 222 No. 33.
B31.6.p: Giant birds of various other kinds that are not otherwise classified, appearing as huge mythical birds in folk stories.

B31.6.1.p: A giant bird that is black, appearing as a huge mythical blackbird.

B31.6.2.p: A giant bird pulls an oak tree up out of the ground, roots and all.

B31.6.2.1.p: When a giant bird lands on an oak tree, the tree shakes and trembles.

B32.r: *Hdwb. d. deutschen Aberglaubens I 180; *Gunkel Das Märchen im alten Testament 36f.; Roscher Lexikon III 3450 s. v. “Phoinix”.—Fb “phoenix”.—Medieval Romance: Wells Manual of Writings 105 (Prose Alexander).—Chinese: Ferguson 98, Eberhard FFC CXX 117 No. 73; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
B32.p: The phoenix, a mythical bird that appears in folk stories.

B32.1.p: The phoenix makes itself young again, restoring its youth.

B32.1.1.p: The phoenix renews its youth when it reaches the age of 1,000 years.

B33.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 84; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 72.
B33.p: Mythical birds that devour people and kill humans.

B33.1.p: Other mythical birds that cause destruction and ruin, not classed as man-eaters.

B33.1.1.p: Destructive birds wither everything they breathe on, killing plants and life around them with their breath.

B33.1.2.p: Destructive birds destroy the grass wherever they go.

B33.1.3.p: Black birds destroy the crops in the fields.

B33.1.4.p: Destructive birds carry poisonous spells on their wings that harm whatever they touch.

B34.p: A mythical bird of dawn with golden feathers and three feet.

B35.r: Carries off the people’s enemies.—Persian: Carnoy 289; Penzer I 103.
B35.p: Camrosh, a giant bird that gathers seeds and makes sure they are placed properly.

B36.p: A mythical bird that produces milk.

B37.r: (cf. B32.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
B37.p: A mythical bird that cannot die and lives forever.

B39.p: Mythical birds of other kinds not classed elsewhere in the index.

B39.1.p: A bird that comes from paradise, a heavenly or magical bird.

B40.p: Creatures that are part bird and part beast, combining features of both animals.

B41.p: A mythical creature that combines a horse and a bird, with the body of a horse and the wings or flight of a bird.

B41.1.p: Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth, a type of bird-horse.

B41.2.r: *Chauvin V 228 No. 130; Fb “hest” IV 211a; BP II 134; *Hdwb. d. deutschen Märchens s. v. “Arabische Motive”; Penzer II 224; Rösch FFC LXXVII 110—Icel.: MacCulloch Eddic 43 (Sleipnir), 185 (Hofvarpnir).—Arabian: Burton I 160, V 246 n., VI 8, VII 46, 53, S II 85; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 838, 1358; Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 314.
B41.2.p: A horse that flies through the air, either because it has wings or because magic carries it aloft.

B41.2.1.p: A flying horse that pulls the chariot of angels.

B42.r: *Chauvin VII 13 No. 313B; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 1129f.; Penzer I 104, 141 n. 2; Irish myth: Cross; Icel.: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
B42.p: A griffin, a mythical beast with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle.

B42.1.r: Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 232.
B42.1.p: A hippogriff, a creature with a horse's body and the front half of a griffin.

B43.r: Spence Myths of Bab. & Assyr. 289f.; India: Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman.
B43.p: A winged bull, a bull that has wings and can fly.

B43.1.p: A flying buffalo, a buffalo that can fly through the air.

B44.p: A bird-bear, a mythical creature that combines a bear with a bird.

B45.p: An elephant that travels through the air.

B46.r: Old English: Solomon and Saturnus (Grein-Wülcker) III (2) 58—82, lines 262ff.
B46.p: Vasa Mortis, a monstrous bird with four heads, a whale-like middle, and the feathers and feet of a griffin.

B47.p: A winged camel, a camel that has wings and can fly.

B48.p: A flying crustacean, a shellfish or crab-like creature that can fly through the air.

B49.p: Miscellaneous flying bird-beasts that do not fit the other categories in this group.

B49.1.p: A bird with the head of a crocodile.

B49.2.p: A flying ape, an ape that can fly through the air.

B49.3.p: A flying fox, a fox that can fly through the air.

B50.p: Bird-men, mythical beings that are part human and part bird.

B51.r: **Laistner Rätsel der Sphinx; *Frazer Apollodorus I 349 n. 1; **J. Ilberg Die Sphinx in der griechischen Kunst und Saga (Leipzig, 1896); Köhler-Bolte I 115.
B51.p: A sphinx, a creature with a woman's face, a lion's body and tail, and a bird's wings.

B52.r: Greek: Fox 111, *Grote I 216f.; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 564.
B52.p: A harpy, a bird creature with the arms and breasts of a woman.

B53.r: *Encyclopaedia Britannica s.v. “sirens”; Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 310 n. 1 (here considered as half fish, half woman); Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Seirenen”; Penzer VI 282 n. 6; *Frazer Apollodorus I 21, II 291 n. 2; *Weicker Der Seelenvogel in d. alten Literatur und Kunst.—Slavic: Máchal 260; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 41 No. 26.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “sirène”; Gascon: Bladé II 342 No. 10; Jewish: Neuman.
B53.p: A siren: a mythical bird with a woman's head who lures sailors with her song.

B53.0.1.p: A siren who appears in the form of a mermaid, a woman with a fish's tail.

B53.1.p: A siren saves a man who is drowning, pulling him out of the water.

B53.2.p: A siren nurses a man, giving him milk from her breast.

B53.3.p: A siren throws gold onto the shore for people to find.

B53.4.p: A siren's song puts listeners to sleep.

B55.p: A mythical creature that is a man with a bird's head.

B56.r: *Penzer I 103, VII 56 n. X 159; Chauvin V 228, VII 12.—Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 345.—Indonesian: Dixon 224.—Panchatantra (trans. Ryder) 94ff.; Penzer-Tawney X 159 “Garuda”.
B56.p: The garuda, a mythical bird-being whose lower body is a man and whose upper body is a bird.

B57.p: The finngalkn, a mythical bird with a man's head.

B60.p: A mythical fish, a fantastic sea creature of unusual size or form.

B60.1.p: A mythical fish that is the ancestor of all other fishes.

B61.r: Giant fish.—Hebrew: Job 41:1, Psalms 104:26, Isaiah 27:1; Jewish: *Neuman.—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
B61.p: Leviathan, a huge sea monster of enormous size.

B62.p: A fish that can fly through the air.

B63.p: A mythical octopus, a giant or fantastic sea creature with many arms.

B64.p: A mythical eel, a fantastic giant or magical eel.

B65.p: A mythical shark, a fantastic or monstrous shark.

B68.r: S. A. Indian (Chaco): Beliaeff BBAE CXLIII (1) 379.
B68.p: A water monster with horns on its head.

B70.p: Mythical beasts that are part fish, living in or related to the water.

B71.r: *Chauvin VII 7 No. 373a n. 1; *Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 133ff.; Tobler Epiphanie der Seele 97.—Irish myth: Cross; Scotch: MacDougall and Calder 309ff.; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 42 No. 31.—Chinese: Ferguson 30.
B71.p: A sea horse: a horse that lives in the sea.

B72.r: Irish myth: Cross.—Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 42 No. 32; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn (1893) 153ff., (1928) 105ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
B72.p: A sea cow: a cow that lives in the sea.

B72.1.p: A mythical animal in the form of three sea-cows, one red, one white, and one black.

B210.p: Animals talk like humans in the story. This is the general heading for tales in which beasts speak.

B210.1.r: Example: Man riding horse and followed by dog tells horse to jump over a hole. B240.2.r: Chuh (Indians of Guatemala): Kunst JAFL XXVIII 353 No. 1; India: Thompson-Balys.
B240.2.p: The rabbit is named king of the animals.

B240.3.p: A wild man is named king of the animals.

B240.4.r: (Cf. K961, K962, K1632.)—Wienert FFC LVI 47; Benfey Panchatantra I 91, 230; Bødker Exempler 277 No. 17, 303 No. 74; Jewish: Neuman; Graf FFC XXXVII passim; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
B240.4.p: The lion is named king of the animals.

B240.4.1.p: When the lion is king of the animals, his chief minister or adviser is a crane.

B240.5.p: The tortoise is named king of the animals.

B240.6.r: Africa (Luba): De Clerq Zs. f. Kolonialspr. IV 195f. No. 8.
B240.6.p: The gazelle is named king of the animals.

B240.7.r: Africa (Luba): De Clerq Zs. f. Kolonialspr. IV 198ff. No. 10.
B240.7.p: The buffalo is named king of the animals.

B240.8.p: The fox is named or made ruler over all the animals. The tale says the fox holds kingship over the beasts.

B240.9.p: The dog is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.10.p: The wolf is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.11.p: The camel is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.12.p: The monkey is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.13.p: The tiger is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.14.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Fang): Trilles 175, (Cameroon): Mansfield passim.
B240.14.p: The elephant is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B240.15.p: The crocodile is named or made ruler over all the animals.

B241.p: Some beast or animal is made king over the four-footed beasts. The tale centers on kingship among quadrupeds.

B241.1.p: Various different beasts are each said to be king of the beasts. The tale gives different animals this title.

B241.2.p: A particular animal is made king over the various kinds of beasts, with each kind under its rule. The tale describes a king ruling several animal kinds.

B241.2.1.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “roi”; Malone PMLA XLIII 409.
B241.2.1.p: A lion is king over the lions, the animal kind it rules.

B241.2.2.r: Cowell Jataka III 225 No. 407; Penzer V 127ff.; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 287; Chinese: Eberhard 40 No. 27, 411 s.v. “Affenkönig”.
B241.2.2.p: A king is set over the monkeys, ruling the monkey kind.

B241.2.3.r: Fb “kattekonge”.—English: Jacobs More Eng. 237; Irish myth: Cross.
B241.2.3.p: A king is set over the cats, ruling the cat kind.

B241.2.4.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “rats”; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 28 No. 12.
B241.2.4.p: A king is set over the rats, ruling the rat kind.

B241.2.5.p: A king is set over the mice, ruling the mouse kind.

B241.2.6.p: A king is set over the hares, ruling the hare kind.

B241.2.7.p: A king is set over the dogs, ruling the dog kind.

B241.2.8.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair West African Folk-Tales 105ff. No. 19.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
B241.2.8.p: A king is set over the tigers, ruling the tiger kind.

B241.2.8.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 161.
B241.2.8.1.p: Newly born divine twins are cared for by a mother-of-tigers, a tiger mother who raises them. The tale features divine infants nursed by a tigress.

B241.2.9.p: A jackal is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the jackal as king of the wild animals.

B241.2.10.p: A deer is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the deer as king of the wild animals.

B241.2.11.r: Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 275, 308; Wienert FFC LVI 47; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 415, 483, 921.
B241.2.11.p: An elephant is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the elephant as king of the wild animals.

B241.2.12.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 986, II 819f.
B241.2.12.p: A boar is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the boar as king of the wild animals.

B241.2.13.p: An antelope is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the antelope as king of the wild animals.

B241.2.14.r: Africa (Ganda): Rowling Tales of Sir Apolo 44ff.
B241.2.14.p: A mongoose is recognized as the ruler of all the beasts. The motif names the mongoose as king of the wild animals.

B241.3.p: A man who has been changed into an animal becomes the leader of a herd or group of four-footed beasts.

B242.r: *Type 221; *BP III 278 (Gr. No. 171).—Irish myth: Cross; Bødker Exempler 293, No. 52.; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “oiseaux”; Missouri-French: Carrière; English: Jacobs English 82 No. 17; Hindu: Tawney I 183, II 65 n.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 40, 437.
B242.p: A bird is recognized as the ruler of all the birds. This is the general heading for tales where the birds choose or win a king.

B242.1.p: Different kinds of birds are named as king of the birds in various tales.

B242.1.1.p: The eagle is made king of the birds.

B242.1.2.r: (Cf. B236.1.)—*Type 221; *BP III 278 (Gr. No. 171); Irish myth: Cross; Japanese: Ikeda.
B242.1.2.p: The wren is made king of the birds, usually by winning a contest for the kingship.

B242.1.2.1.p: The wren is called a druid of the birds, using an Irish-language title for this role.

B242.1.3.p: The hornbill is made king of the birds.

B242.1.4.r: Africa (Duala): Gehr Zs. f. Kolonialspr. VII 25ff.
B242.1.4.p: The pelican is made king of the birds.

B242.1.5.r: Madagascar (Merina): Renel Contes de Madagascar II 160ff. No. 100.
B242.1.5.p: The shrike is made king of the birds.

B242.1.6.p: The jackdaw is made king of the birds.

B242.1.7.p: The peacock is made king of the birds.

B242.1.8.p: The owl is made king of the birds.

B242.1.9.p: The swan is made king of the birds.

B242.1.10.p: The ziz, a huge mythical bird, is made king of the birds.

B242.2.p: A bird is made or accepted as ruler over all the various kinds of birds.

B242.2.1.p: The crow is made king over the birds.

B242.2.2.p: The dove is made king over the birds.

B242.2.3.p: The kite (a bird of prey) is made king over the birds.

B242.2.4.p: The pigeon is made king over the birds.

B242.2.5.p: The peacock is made king over the birds.

B242.2.6.p: The quail is made king over the birds.

B242.2.7.p: The sparrow is made king over the birds.

B242.2.8.p: The parrot is made king over the birds.

B242.2.9.p: The goose is made king over the birds.

B242.2.10.p: The swan is made king over the birds.

B242.2.11.p: The vulture is made king over the birds.

B242.2.12.p: The lark is made king over the birds.

B243.r: (Cf. B236.2.) *Type 303; *BP I 528, III 284 (Gr. No. 172); *Dh IV 192ff.; Hartland Science 174.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “poisson”; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Africa (Angola): Chatelain 65 No. 3; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 6, 52.
B243.p: A fish is made or accepted as ruler over all fishes.

B243.1.p: Various different fishes are each said to be king of the fishes, in different versions of the story.

B243.1.1.p: The herring is made king of the fishes.

B243.1.2.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 6.
B243.1.2.p: The eel is made king of the fishes.

B243.1.3.p: The shark is made king of the fishes.

B243.2.p: A king is set over various kinds of fishes, as a ruler of the fish kinds collectively.

B243.2.1.p: The salmon is made king over the various kinds of fishes.

B243.2.2.p: A tale in which an eel is the ruler or chief of all eels or of fishes in general, portrayed as a king among the creatures of the water.

B244.p: A reptile is portrayed as the ruler or king of all reptiles.

B244.1.r: *Type 672; BP II 463f.; *Fb “snogekonge” III 437b, “lindorm” II 433 b, “hugormekonge” I 667.—Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 213ff., (1928) 139ff.—Hindu: Keith 154; Penzer VI 29; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 27, 64, 230, 1149, II 529, 556; Chinese: Eberhard 17 No. 8; Zanzibar: Bateman 202 No. 10.
B244.1.p: A snake is portrayed as the ruler or king of all serpents.

B244.1.1.p: A female ruler, a queen, is portrayed as the sovereign of the water snakes.

B244.1.2.p: The serpent king is said to live in a lake or pool.

B244.1.3.p: The serpent king is described as having an enormously large hood, the spreading neck-shield of a cobra.

B244.1.4.p: Snakes are said to be divided into four royal families, each with its own ruling line.

B244.2.p: A naga, a serpent being of folk belief, is portrayed as a king who rules over the nagas or serpents.

B244.3.p: A lizard is portrayed as the ruler or king of all lizards.

B245.p: An amphibian is portrayed as the ruler or king of all amphibians.

B245.1.r: Type 440, Grimm No. 1; BP I 1ff.; Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 369; Bødker Exempler 297 No. 61; Cosquin Études 530; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “roi”, “grenouille”.—English: Jacobs English 237; Hindu: Keith 147; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard 76 No. 43.
B245.1.p: A frog is portrayed as the ruler or king of all frogs.

B245.2.p: A turtle is portrayed as the ruler or king of the turtles.

B246.p: An insect is portrayed as the ruler or king of all insects.

B246.1.p: An ant is portrayed as the ruler or king of all ants.

B246.2.p: A fly is portrayed as the ruler, a king or sultan, of all flies.

B246.3.p: A bee is portrayed as the ruler or king of all bees.

B248.p: A dragon is portrayed as the ruler or king of all dragons.

B250.r: Günter Christliche Legende des Abendlandes 80ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 334; Jewish: Neuman.
B250.p: Animals are portrayed as having religious life, acting in ways that resemble worship or devotion, as humans do.

B251.p: Animals are portrayed as praising God or a sacred power, or as worshipping in some way.

B251.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; English: Child V 485 s.v. “joy”.
B251.1.p: Animals are portrayed as rejoicing and celebrating at the birth of Christ.

B251.1.1.r: *Dh II 12ff.—Alphabet No. 554.—Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
B251.1.1.p: Animals adore the newborn Jesus, bowing or worshipping him at his birth.

B251.1.2.r: DeCock Volkskunde XXI 52ff.; Luzel Légendes Chretiennes de la Basse Bretagne II 333; Tille Die Geschichte der deutschen Weinacht 66f.; Wossidlo Mecklenbürgische Volksüberlieferung II (1) 59, 369; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *748; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 47 No. 237; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 637.
B251.1.2.p: At Christmas, animals are heard talking to each other, often about the birth of Christ.

B251.1.2.1.p: A rooster crows the Latin announcement that Christ has been born.

B251.1.2.2.p: Cows are heard speaking to one another on Christmas.

B251.1.2.3.p: Cows kneel in their stable at midnight on the eve of Old Christmas.

B251.2.p: Animals show honor and reverence to a saint or holy churchman.

B251.2.1.p: Animals sing in praise of a saint.

B251.2.2.p: Fish hold races to give a saint a welcome.

B251.2.3.p: Wolves lick a saint's shoes out of reverence.

B251.2.4.p: A fly regularly buzzes whenever a churchman comes back from morning prayers.

B251.2.5.p: Birds beat the water with their wings to welcome a saint.

B251.2.6.p: Deer lick a saint's tomb every day at noon.

B251.2.6.2.p: A cow licks a saint's feet.

B251.2.7.p: Wild animals behave as the disciples or followers of a saint.

B251.2.7.1.p: Fish gather in great numbers at a stream bank to listen to Anthony of Padua preaching.

B251.2.8.p: A sea monster honors one saint above all others.

B251.2.9.p: Birds mourn when a saint leaves them.

B251.2.10.p: A cow gives twelve measures of milk for the twelve apostles of Ireland.

B251.2.10.1.p: A brilliantly white cow comes to be milked for an infant saint.

B251.2.11.p: A lion lies down at the feet of a saint in a gesture of humble reverence.

B251.2.12.p: Birds gather and take part in the funeral of a saint.

B251.3.r: Jewish: Neuman (cow, cat, lion, mouse, cock, vulture, fish, frog); Irish myth: Cross.
B251.3.p: Animals sing songs of praise, as if worshipping God or a holy figure.

B251.3.1.r: Patch PMLA XXXIII 626 n. 89; Irish myth: Cross.
B251.3.1.p: In the otherworld, birds sing religious songs.

B251.4.p: Animals pray to God or to a holy figure.

B251.4.1.p: An animal asks a saint for protection.

B251.4.1.1.p: A wild animal seeks a saint's protection from hunters, going to the saint for safety.

B251.5.p: Animals fast, going without food as a religious discipline.

B251.6.p: Animals keep religious rules and commandments.

B251.7.p: An animal makes a solemn religious oath.

B251.7.1.p: A wolf swears an oath by God.

B251.8.p: Animals respect a sacred revelation, behaving as if a holy message has been received.

B251.8.1.p: Birds stop singing at the moment a sacred revelation is given.

B251.9.p: Animals give religious responses, such as answering in worship or ritual.

B252.p: Animals who act as churchmen, holding religious office or living in religious roles.

B252.1.r: Irish: Plummer Vitae Sanctorum Hiberniae cxli.; Irish myth: Cross.

B252.2.p: In the otherworld, birds call the hours of prayer, as church bells would.

B252.3.p: A snake that acts as a priest over snakes.

B253.p: Animals perform the rites and duties of the church, such as conducting services.

B253.1.p: Snakes take part in a religious ceremony or rite, such as a holy gathering with a sacred function.

B253.2.p: Wolves celebrate a yearly church feast day, as people do.

B253.3.p: A fox goes without food as a religious penance or self-punishment for sin.

B253.4.p: A spider does penance, performing a religious act of self-punishment to atone for wrongdoing.

B253.5.p: A deer carries a cross between its antlers, as a sign of Christian faith.

B253.6.p: A deer has lit candles fixed on the tips of its antlers.

B255.p: A miracle is performed for an animal, so that a holy person or divine power helps it in a supernatural way.

B256.r: (Cf. B292.)—*Loomis White Magic 63; Irish myth: Cross; Irish: Plummer cxliiff.
B256.p: An animal serves a saint, helping or obeying a holy person as a servant.

B256.0.1.p: An animal is tricked or fooled by a saint, who uses deception on it.

B256.1.r: Saints’ legend (Irish): Plummer cxlvi.; Irish myth: Cross.
B256.1.p: Birds build their nests in a saint's hand or in his monk's hood (cowl).

B256.1.1.p: Birds perch on the hands and head of a saint, showing he is trusted by them.

B256.2.p: Pigs that have been dedicated to a saint are considered sacred and are treated with respect.

B256.3.p: A deer offers its antlers to a saint to hold his book up while he reads.

B256.3.1.p: Deer provide a bier to carry a saint's corpse and bring it to the church for burial.

B256.4.p: Wolves are tamed and kept as domestic animals by a saint.

B256.4.1.p: While a saint is away, wolves guard his cattle like watchdogs.

B256.5.p: Birds obey a saint's commands, doing what he tells them.

B256.5.1.p: Birds protect a saint and perform services for him.

B256.6.p: A wild boar serves a saint as a helper or servant.

B256.6.1.p: A boar guards a holy man's pigs, keeping watch over his herd.

B256.6.2.p: A boar plays music for a holy man, serving him as a kind of servant because of his saintliness.

B256.6.3.p: A boar acts as a doctor for a holy man, licking his injured feet to heal them.

B256.7.p: A tiger sweeps the temple floor for a saint, performing a menial task in his service.

B256.8.p: A wolf brings back a child that was taken, because of a saint's prayer.

B256.9.p: Stags pull a plow for a saint, doing the work of oxen in his fields.

B256.10.p: A fly, a wren and a fox live with a cleric, sharing his home as companions.

B256.11.p: A wolf returns sheep that it had stolen from a saint, restoring the stolen flock.

B256.12.p: A whale raises its back so that voyaging clerics can land on it and hold a celebration.

B257.p: Animals hold a funeral, mourning or burying one of their own in a manner like human rites.

B259.p: A collection of miscellaneous tales in which animals behave in religious ways, such as observing church rules.

B259.1.r: Hebrew: Gaster Exempla 228 No. 235; Jewish: Neuman.
B259.1.p: An ass insists that food be tithed, refusing to eat when thieves who stole it have not paid the church tenth of their provisions.

B259.2.r: Jewish: Bin Gorion Born Judas@2 II 92, *342; Jewish: Neuman.
B259.2.p: A cow observes the Sabbath and refuses to work on that holy day.

B259.3.p: A hog refuses food offered by men who have been excommunicated from the church.

B259.4.r: (Cf. A2012.1.)—*Kittredge Witchcraft 150, 469 n. 112; Alphabet No. 695.—*Loomis White Magic 65.—Irish myth: Cross.
B259.4.p: Bees build a small church of wax to hold the consecrated Host, the bread of the Eucharist.

B259.4.1.p: Animals do not spoil or harm the consecrated food kept in the bees' wax church.

B259.5.p: A bird's wings drip blood when the birds hear that the Day of Judgment is coming.

B260.p: Tales of wars fought among animals, in which creatures take sides and battle one another.

B260.1.r: Tahltan: Teit JAFL XXXII 213 No. 1 (18); Shuswap: Teit JE II 658f.
B260.1.p: Two groups of animals agree to a peace treaty, ending their hostilities.

B261.r: *Type 222; BP II 435 (Gr. No. 102); *Dh III 3ff., 226, IV 197ff.—Crane Vitry No. 153; Scala Celi No. 417. Japanese: Ikeda.—Africa: Frobenius Atlantis VIII 253, IX 115, XI 128.
B261.p: A war breaks out between birds and four-legged animals.

B261.1.r: Discredited.—Wienert FFC LVI *48 (ET 66, 67), *52 (ET 166), 134 (ST 398, 399); Halm Aesop Nos. 307, 391; Dh IV 197ff.; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Benga): Nassau 163 No. 21, (Ibo, Nigeria): Basden 281, Thomas 161 (hornbill), (Mpongwe): Nassau 53 No. 8 (crocodile), (Yoruba): Ellis 252 No. 3.
B261.1.p: A bat takes part in a war between birds and four-footed animals, joining first one side and then the other because of its ambiguous shape.

B261.1.1.p: A tame elephant is rejected by its wild relatives, who will not accept it back among them.

B262.p: A war in which tame animals fight against wild animals.

B263.p: A war between two or more groups of animals other than the domestic-versus-wild pairing.

B263.1.p: A war in which toads and frogs fight against each other.

B263.2.p: A war in which elephants and ants fight against each other.

B263.3.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Hindu: Penzer V 98—113.—Panchatantra III intr. (tr. Ryder) 291ff; Bødker Exempler 293 No. 52.
B263.3.p: A war in which crows and owls fight against each other.

B263.4.p: A war in which birds and reptiles fight against each other.

B263.5.p: A war between two groups of birds.

B263.5.1.p: A war in which birds fight against an eagle.

B263.6.p: A war in which monkeys and grasshoppers fight against each other.

B263.7.p: A war in which serpents and storks fight against each other.

B263.8.p: A war in which a lion fights against other animals.

B264.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48.—Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 116.—Icel.: *Boberg; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
B264.p: A one-on-one fight between two animals.

B264.1.p: An animal fights a pack of hounds.

B264.2.p: An eagle and a fish fight each other.

B264.3.p: A buffalo and a tiger fight a duel; in the buffalo's case it arms itself for the fight.

B264.4.p: A snake and a millipede fight each other.

B264.5.p: An ape and a tortoise fight each other.

B265.p: Animals keep tearing each other apart in constant fighting.

B266.1.p: Cattle that are thirsty fight over a well.

B267.p: Animals join together as allies in a war or fight against a common enemy.

B267.1.p: A dog and a wolf form an alliance with each other, joining forces as partners.

B267.2.p: A sheep and a dog form an alliance, banding together as partners.

B267.3.p: A raven and a crow form an alliance, joining together as partners.

B267.4.p: A rooster and a seabird form an alliance, joining together as partners.

B268.p: Animals serve as soldiers, fighting in an army or battle as if they were human troops.

B268.1.r: Hindu: Keith 128; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 328 (monkeys).
B268.1.p: A large army made up of apes fights in a battle or war.

B268.2.p: A group of dogs serves as mounted fighters, like a cavalry unit in battle.

B268.2.1.p: Dogs trained to fight in war serve as soldiers on the battlefield.

B268.3.p: Elephants are used as soldiers and fighting beasts in war.

B268.4.p: A sorcerer commands an army made of animals he has enchanted or made magical.

B268.5.p: A large army made up of birds fights in a battle or war.

B268.5.1.p: An army made up of quails fights in a battle or war.

B268.6.p: A large army made up of mice fights in a battle or war.

B268.7.p: A large army made up of snakes fights in a battle or war.

B268.7.1.p: An army made up of snakes and scorpions fights in a battle or war.

B268.8.p: A large army made up of insects fights in a battle or war.

B268.8.1.p: An army made up of hornets fights in a battle or war.

B268.8.2.p: An army made up of locusts fights in a battle or war.

B268.8.3.p: An army made up of wasps fights in a battle or war.

B268.9.p: An army made up of tigers, which the animals raise and send into battle as soldiers.

B268.10.p: An army made up of cows, which animals raise and send into battle as soldiers.

B268.11.p: An army made up of cats, which animals raise and send into battle as soldiers.

B268.12.p: An army made up of wild boars, which animals raise and send into battle as soldiers.

B268.13.p: An army made up of hyenas, which animals raise and send into battle as soldiers.

B270.r: **Cabanès Les animaux en justice (L’indiscretions de l’histoire, 5e serie, procedures singulières, Paris, 1920), **Lossouarn Les animaux en justice aux temps jadis (Bordeaux 1905).—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Bødker Exempler 289 No. 40, 294 No. 55.; Jewish: Neuman.
B270.p: Animals take part in legal matters, such as lawsuits, trials, and judgments, as if they were people.

B270.1.p: The owl and the kite bring a lawsuit against each other before a court.

B270.2.p: The owl brings a lawsuit against the mouse, and the two argue their case in court.

B271.p: Animals bring lawsuits of their own against people or other parties, acting as plaintiffs.

B271.1.p: A parrot and a sparrow go to court to argue over who should inherit the property a man left behind. The sparrow claims the same interest as the man, while the parrot argues it caused the man's wealth by letting him sell its feathers; the people decide for the parrot.

B271.2.p: A cat that has been injured is awarded grain as payment for the harm done to it.

B271.3.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 648; *Wesselski Theorie 20; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
B271.3.p: Animals ring a bell to call the king and demand justice. The bell is a royal bell that petitioners may ring; in some versions a serpent rings it while threatened by a turtle, or an old horse rings it to complain about a cruel master.

B272.p: Animals are brought to court as defendants and are judged or made to answer for their actions.

B272.1.p: A lawsuit is brought against an animal, which must defend itself in court.

B272.2.r: *Evans (E.P.) The criminal Prosecution and Capital punishment of Animals (New York 1926), von Amira (K). Tierstrafen und Tierprozesse (Innsbruck, 1891); *Mittheilungen d. Instituts f. öster. Geschichtsforsch. XII (1891) 545; *H. A. Berkenhoff Tierstrafe, Tierbannung und rechtsrituelle Tiertötung im Mittelalter (Strassburg 1937, diss.); Fb “stævne”.
B272.2.p: An animal is put on trial for a crime it is accused of committing.

B272.2.1.p: A horse is put on trial for a crime it is accused of committing.

B274.r: Africa: Milligan 98. (See all references to J1172.3. and J1130. Cleverness in law court.)
B274.p: An animal serves as a judge who hears cases and decides them.

B275.r: Wesselski Nasreddin I 208 No. 11, II 186 No. 356.—*Von Amira Tierstrafen und Tierprozesse (Innsbruck, 1891); Jewish: Neuman.
B275.p: An animal is punished for something it has done, as a person would be.

B275.1.r: *Frazer Old Testament III 415—445; *Wesselski Märchen 231; **Evans The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals (New York, 1906); Grimm Rechtsaltertümer II 235; Sébillot France III 27; Wilken Verspreide Geschriften IV 181ff.; Jewish: Neuman.
