B498.1.r: (Cf. B11.)—Italian Novella: Rotunda, Swiss Jegerlehner Oberwallis 328 No. 17; Chinese: Graham.
B498.1.p: A dragon helps the hero, rather than threatening him. It is a mythical creature acting as a friendly helper.

B500.r: Type 675; Fb “ønske” III 1179a.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Missouri French: Carrière; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 317 n. 146c; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 71 No. 3. (Cf. B100—B199 Magic animals.)
B500.p: Animals give a person magical power or help of a supernatural kind. This group covers the various ways animals provide such services.

B501.r: *Types 531, 552, 553; BP III 18ff., 424ff.; Malone PMLA XLIII 407; *Fb “fjer” I 301, “hår” I 771b.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v “talisman”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 15; Missouri-French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.—Persian: Carnoy 290, 331.—Africa (Kaffir): Theal 85, (Swahili): Steere 199; N. A. Indian (Pawnee): Dorsey MAFLS VIII 102.
B501.p: An animal gives the hero a part of its body, such as a horn, feather, or jewel, as a token. The hero can use this token to call the animal back when he needs help.

B501.1.p: Buffalo give the hero horns that he can blow to summon them to his aid.

B501.1.1.p: The buffalo give the hero two horns: a merry horn, blown when all is well, and an angry horn, blown when he is in trouble. Each horn calls the buffalo in the matching situation.

B501.2.p: A kite teaches the hero a rhyme or verse, and by reciting it the hero can call the kite to help him.

B501.3.p: An animal gives the hero a jewel, which he can use to summon the animal whenever he needs help.

B501.4.p: Birds give the hero a feather, which he can burn when he is in difficulty to bring the birds to help him.

B505.r: *Types 560, 561; *Aarne MSFO XXV 3—82; BP II 451ff., 537; Type 554*; *Köhler-Bolte I 440; Hartland Perseus III 199; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “talisman”; Missouri-French: Carrière.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 37 No. 24.—Africa (Zanzibar): Bateman 221 No. 10, (Basuto): Jacottet 214 No. 31. See also references in B375.1.
B505.p: A person receives a magic object from an animal. The object then gives the person some supernatural power or benefit.

B505.1.p: A person receives a magic object from an animal who is a brother-in-law, that is, an animal related by marriage to the hero.

B505.2.p: An animal tells the hero where to find a magic object he needs.

B505.3.p: A fish gives the hero a magic song, which gives him supernatural power or help.

B510.p: Animals heal people or cure their injuries and illnesses. This group covers the various ways animals provide healing.

B511.p: An animal acts as a healer, curing a sick or injured person through its own powers or knowledge.

B511.1.r: *Chauvin VII 25 No. 373 F note 5; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 648; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
B511.1.p: A snake acts as a healer, curing people of injury or illness.

B511.1.1.r: Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 132 No. 78; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 46 No. 78.
B511.1.1.p: A snake crawls into a man's mouth and so heals him.

B511.1.2.p: A snake heals a maiden who has been mutilated, using magic herbs.

B511.1.3.p: A hedgehog helps a raja who has been bitten by a snake. It forces the snake to suck the poison out of the raja's body.

B511.2.p: A magical pig acts as a healer who cures injuries and illnesses. It is one form of the animal healer motif.

B511.2.1.p: A magical pig heals a wound merely by having its skin touch the injury.

B511.2.2.p: A magical pig heals wounds by licking them.

B511.3.p: A loyal horse pushes a sleep-causing thorn out of its master's head, waking him up.

B511.4.r: S. A. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE 143 III 685.
B511.4.p: A rat heals a man's wound.

B511.5.r: Chinese-Persian: Coyajee JPASB XXIV 185f.; Alu: Wheeler 60; Papua: Ker 103.
B511.5.p: A bird heals a man, restoring him to health.

B511.5.1.p: A vulture cures a man's blindness.

B512.r: (Cf. B491.)—*Type 160, 303, 590, 612; *BP I 128; Chauvin II 106 No. 71; Kittredge Gawain 153 n. 4; Wesselski Märchen 239f. No. 50.—*Krappe Papers and Trans. of Jubilee Cong. of Folk-Lore Soc. 277ff.—*Fb “blad” IV 44a; *Frazer Apollodorus I 312 n. 2.—Icel.: Boberg, Völsunga saga ch. 8.; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda. N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 354 n. 279.
B512.p: An animal treats another animal with a herb, water, or other remedy, thereby showing a human the cure. Sometimes the remedy brings the dead back to life. The animal is most often a serpent.

B513.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Missouri-French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.—See references for B235.
B513.p: A hero learns how to cure his own blindness and a king's or princess's sickness by overhearing a meeting of animals who discuss the remedy.

B514.p: An animal goes out and fetches a remedy to cure a man.

B514.1.p: A grateful fox fetches a fox's liver to serve as a remedy for a man.

B514.2.p: A bee brings healing balm from heaven to restore the hero's speech.

B514.3.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 163 No. 32.
B514.3.p: A snake gives a man an antidote to cure poison.

B515.r: *Types 300, 665. Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
B515.p: Animals bring a dead person back to life.

B516.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 31, Rasmussen I 312, III 203, Rink 100, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 169, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 169, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 626.
B516.p: An animal restores a person's sight.

B520.r: See also B540.—Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 372 n. 1 (horse).—Icel.: *Boberg; Missouri-French: Carrière; Panchatantra III 8 (tr. Ryder) 334; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1260; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 25, 28, 31, 84; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen 76.
B520.p: Animals rescue a person from death or serious harm.

B521.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Jewish: Neuman; U.S.: Baughman; Africa (Duala): Lederbogen Märchen 75, (Fang): Trilles 138, (Loango): Pechuël-Loesche 109.
B521.p: An animal warns a person of a danger that would otherwise be fatal.

B521.1.r: Fable: Halm Aesop No. 120, Wienert FFC LVI 70 (ET 338), 127 (ST 353), (eagle).—India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 76 No. 12 (ox).
B521.1.p: An animal warns a person not to eat or drink something poisoned.

B521.1.1.p: A horse advises the hero not to wash in water, as his false wife has told him to, because his eyes will pop out.

B521.1.2.p: An animal warns a man not to drink something.

B521.2.p: An animal gives a warning that saves a person from an accident.

B521.2.1.r: Fable: Babrius No. 144, Halm Aesop No. 92, Wienert FFC 70 (ET 339), 127 (ST 353).
B521.2.1.p: An eagle rescues a man from a collapsing wall by snatching his hat and drawing him away from it. The eagle does this as a reward for the man's earlier kindness.

B521.3.r: Icel.: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 87.
B521.3.p: Animals warn a person that an attack is coming, allowing them to escape or defend themselves.

B521.3.1.r: Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 270 No. 82; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 452.
B521.3.1.p: Dogs bark or otherwise alert a person to the presence of a witch who means harm.

B521.3.2.p: Geese make a loud cackling that raises the alarm and warns of danger.

B521.3.3.p: A flea bites a sleeping king and wakes him while a robber is breaking in to rob him. The robber had earlier told the flea of his plan.

B521.3.3.1.p: A fly lands on a sleeping prince's nose and wakes him just in time to save him from an enemy.

B521.3.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 536.
B521.3.4.p: A dog warns a person that they are being pursued.

B521.3.5.p: An owl warns other birds to avoid a net smeared with birdlime, so they do not get trapped.

B521.4.p: Animals warn a man's wife that her husband is in danger.

B521.5.p: An owl flaps its wings to catch a man's attention and so stops him from plunging over a cliff.

B521.6.p: Birds give warning when an enemy is approaching, so people can prepare or escape.

B522.p: An animal saves a man who has been condemned to death.

B522.1.r: B512). By thus ingratiating himself the man is freed from false accusation.—*Type 160; Chauvin II 106 No. 71.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Clouston Tales I 230; Bødker Exempler 304 No. 75; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.—Africa (Vai): Ellis 230 No. 39.
B522.1.p: A serpent bites the prince and then shows a condemned man the cure, so the man saves the prince's life and is spared execution.

B522.2.p: A kite steals jewels from a man who has been wrongly accused and is about to be arrested, carrying them away and so saving him from execution.

B522.3.p: A woman falsely accused of adultery is thrown to lions, but the lions do not harm her.

B522.4.p: An eagle picks up a child who has been condemned to die and carries it away, saving its life.

B522.4.1.p: Cranes circling in the air carry a girl away, saving her from her fate.

B523.p: An animal helps a man escape from someone chasing him.

B523.1.r: (Cf. A2221.5.)—Type 967*; *Dh II 66f.—*Wesselski Theorie 42.—Jewish: Neuman, Bin Gorion; Born Judas@2 III 115ff., Grünbaum Neue Beiträge zur Semitischen Sagenkunde 195; Lappish: Qvigstad Lappiske Eventyr I No. 32, II No. 68.—India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Fang): Trilles 139.
B523.1.p: A spider spins a web over the opening of a hole, making it look undisturbed so that a fugitive hiding inside is not found.

B523.2.p: A whale fights off a monster that is chasing a saint, saving the saint.

B523.3.p: A giant clam pinches or attacks a man who is chasing the hero, stopping the pursuer and saving the hero.

B524.p: An animal defeats an enemy who is threatening a man, saving his life.

B524.1.r: English: Wells Manual of Writings 66 (Ywain and Gawain); Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 98 No. 327; India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 493, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 187.
B524.1.p: Animals defeat a man's enemy through physical force, such as fighting, killing or trampling.

B524.1.1.r: *Type 300; *BP I 547.—Irish myth: Cross; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 20.—Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 56 No. 9, (Zulu): Callaway 51, (Kaffir): Kidd 226 No. 1.
B524.1.1.p: Dogs kill a cannibal or dragon that is attacking a man.

B524.1.2.r: *Parsons Zs. f. Ethnologie LIV 1—29, MAFLS XVII 271 No. 82.—See also most of African references in B421.
B524.1.2.p: Dogs rescue their master, who has fled up a tree to escape them or another danger, by driving off the threat.

B524.1.2.1.p: The dogs break their bonds and kill the man who attacked their master.

B524.1.3.p: A cat kills a rat that is attacking someone.

B524.1.4.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 420; Irish myth: Cross.
B524.1.4.p: A wolf protects its master's child by fighting off a serpent that threatens the child.

B524.1.4.1.p: A dog protects its master's child by fighting off an animal that attacks the child.

B524.1.5.p: Helpful buffaloes trample the hero's enemies to death.

B524.1.5.1.p: Helpful buffaloes rescue the hero by attacking a tiger that threatens him.

B524.1.6.p: A helpful bird kills a snake that is attacking the master's wife and child.

B524.1.7.p: A horse kills enemies who are attacking its master.

B524.1.8.p: A blackbird, trapped with elephants, tells ants to burrow into the elephants' brains, which kills them.

B524.1.9.p: A hawk, grateful to the hero, attacks the hero's enemies.

B524.1.10.p: A helpful centipede kills an ogre.

B524.1.11.p: The hero contests with demons by using fighting animals: a cock, goat, bull, horse, wild bull and peacock.

B524.1.12.p: A crab companion saves the hero from a snake that is about to ravage him.

B524.2.r: Type 545; BP I 325ff., III 487 (Gr. 33a, 214).—Icel.: Boberg; Indonesian: De Vries’ list No. 48.—Africa (Kaffir): Kidd 230 No. 2, (Ekoi): Talbot 233, (Basuto): Jacottet 114 No. 27.
B524.2.p: Animals defeat a man's enemy through cleverness or a planned tactic rather than brute force.

B524.2.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman, Bin Gorion Born Judas@2 III 113ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 323.
B524.2.1.p: Helpful bees or hornets sting an opposing army, defeating it.

B524.2.1.1.p: A saint sends a swarm of bees or wasps to attack the hero's enemies. The insects sting the opposing army.

B524.3.p: A grateful snake protects a man by fighting off an attacker.

B524.4.p: A magical bird stops a mother from killing her baby.

B524.5.p: A broom magically turns into a porcupine and drives away a man who tries to rape a woman.

B524.6.p: A hare, repaying a kindness, gathers an army of animals to help the hero.

B524.7.p: A loyal dog kills a man who plans to murder its sleeping master.

B524.8.p: A chicken pecks out one of an attacker's eyes, helping to save the hero.

B525.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 851.—See all references to B381.
B525.p: An animal that is about to devour a man spares him instead.

B525.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 155, 161, (Carib): ibid. 146.
B525.1.p: A tiger hides a woman from the other tigers so they will not eat her.

B526.p: An animal rescues a man from being burned to death.

B526.1.p: Helpful animals put out the fire that is about to execute the hero, who is to be burned at the stake.

B526.2.p: A helpful mare cools a boiling bath that the hero has been forced to bathe in, by blowing on it.

B527.r: Saints’ legend (Irish): Plummer cxlvi (sea birds); Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 747.
B527.p: An animal rescues a man from drowning.

B527.1.p: A fish promises to spare a man from a coming flood.

B527.2.p: A helpful animal stops a leak in Noah's Ark.

B527.3.p: An owl saves a man from drowning by flapping its wings to show him which way the land is.

B529.p: Miscellaneous cases in which an animal saves a person's life.

B529.1.p: Animals such as a sow, a bitch, or a mare hide a boy inside their bellies to protect him.

B529.2.p: A dragon swallows an arrow, or a thunderbolt, that was aimed at the hero.

B530.r: India: Thompson-Balys.—Zanzibar: Bateman 85 No. 6 (ape, lion, snake).
B530.p: Animals provide men with food, shelter, or other necessities.

B530.1.r: S. A. Indian (Warrau): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 146.
B530.1.p: A magical frog acts as a host and provides food or shelter to a woman.

B530.2.p: Elephants take care of a holy man (ascetic) living alone in the jungle, bringing him food.

B531.r: *Basset 1001 Contes III 295 (birds); *Wesselski Märchen 249 No. 57; Toldo Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. VIII 21; *Fb “hind” I 612 (deer); Alphabet Nos. 361. 636.—Irish myth: Cross, Saints’ legend (Irish): Plummer cxliv (otter).—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “nourriture” (bird, dog); French Canadian: *Barbeau JAFL XXIX 15 (dog); Missouri-French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 328 No 17 (dragon).—Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 217, II 655, 1158; Chinese: Graham; Africa: Stanley 329, (Angola): Chatelain 129 No. 19; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 143, III 80, 198, Rink 227, 413, 462, Holm 84, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 222, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 638, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 176.—S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 6, (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 155.
B531.p: Animals supply food to a person, providing a meal or sustenance when it is needed.

B531.1.r: *Pease Cicero De Divinatione 391 (Bk. I 79), 597; S. A. Indian (Kaiguá): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 139.
B531.1.p: Bees feed babies or infants, giving them nourishment.

B531.2.p: An animal that is milked in an unusual way, so that it yields milk or food from an odd source.

B531.2.1.p: Female deer, tigresses, or she-wolves are milked into a pond until the pond fills with milk.

B531.3.p: A helpful animal retrieves a magic skin that produces food from the bottom of a river.

B531.4.p: A helpful animal accidentally drops a magic food item.

B531.5.p: Birds save a hungry man by throwing themselves into the fire he has built so he can roast and eat them.

B535.r: *Frazer Fasti II 369ff., especially 369 n. 3, 375; Dickson Valentine and Orson 36, 103, 107, 112, 169; *Liebrecht Zur Volkskunde 17ff.; *Nutt FLR IV 1ff.; Penzer II 294; *Fb “ulv” III 971 a (Wolf); *BP II 317, III 60ff.—Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Fox 22 (doe), 56 (bear), 118, 155 (goat, crow, sow), 280, Frazer Apollodorus I 397, II 47 n. 2, Roscher s.v. “Achilleus”; Roman: Fox 307 (Romulus and Remus) (wolf); Persian: Carnoy 330; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chien” (dog); Missouri-French: Carrière; McCartney Papers of Michigan Academy of Science, Arts, and Letters IV (1924) 15—42; Wesselski Theorie 19; Icel.: Þiðriks saga I 302—03 (hind), Boberg; English: Wells 118 (Octovian) (lion); Chinese: Ferguson 41.—N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 387 (Mt. 707), Thompson Tales 316 n. 146b; S. A. Indian (Brazil): Ehrenreich International Congress of Americanists XIV 662.—Indonesian: De Vries Volksverhalen I Nos. 22, 89; India: *Thompson-Balys;—Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 104 No. 15, 190 No. 28, (Wakweli): Bender 49f.
B535.p: An animal serves as a nurse, nourishing an abandoned child.

B535.0.1.p: A cow acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding children.

B535.0.1.1.p: A bison acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding a child.

B535.0.2.p: A bandicoot, a large rat, acts as a nurse for a child.

B535.0.3.p: A goat acts as a nurse, feeding and caring for a child.

B535.0.4.p: A dog acts as a nurse, feeding and caring for a child.

B535.0.5.p: An abandoned prince is raised and grows up in an eagle's nest.

B535.0.6.r: India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Warrau): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 146.
B535.0.6.p: A frog acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding a child.

B535.0.7.p: A bird acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding a child.

B535.0.7.1.p: A stork acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding a child.

B535.0.7.2.p: A crane acts as a nurse, caring for and feeding a child.

B535.0.8.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 161, (Amuesa): ibid. 129.
B535.0.8.p: A tiger acts as a wet nurse, suckling a human child.

B535.0.9.p: A she-wolf acts as a wet nurse, suckling a human child.

B535.0.10.p: Sheep and oxen guard and protect a child who has been left out in the open.

B535.0.11.p: A she-wolf looks after and nourishes a baby that has been abandoned in the forest.

B535.0.12.p: An eagle watches over a baby while the mother is working in the fields.

B535.0.13.r: S. A. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE 143 III 684.
B535.0.13.p: A crab acts as a wet nurse, nourishing a human child.

B535.0.14.r: Greek: Grote I 44; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 529.
B535.0.14.p: A serpent acts as a wet nurse, nourishing a human child.

B535.1.p: A goat feeds other animals from milk inside its body, letting them drink from it internally.

B535.2.p: Animals acting as nurses fight with the real parent over the children.

B536.p: A helpful animal looks after its wounded or sick master, tending and caring for him.

B536.1.p: A helpful bird looks after its master after he has been blinded.

B537.p: Animals take in and care for a mysterious housekeeper who comes to live with them.

B538.p: Animals provide shelter for a person.

B538.1.r: (Cf. B450.)—Irish myth: Cross; Günter Christliche Legende des Abendlandes 125; Singer Zs. f. deutsch. Altertum XXXV 184f.; Dunlop-Wilson History of Fiction I 428; Saintyves Saints Successeurs 134; Dh I 321ff.; Hand. d. Abergl. I 187.—Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 104 No. 15.
B538.1.p: A bird shelters a person by covering them with its wings.

B538.2.r: N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Jones-Michelson PAES VII (1) 77, Carson JAFL XXX 491 No. 1.
B538.2.p: Wolves shelter a man by wrapping him in their tails, so their tails serve as blankets.

B540.p: An animal rescues a person from danger or retrieves a lost object for them.

B540.1.p: Birds drop some of their feathers to a hero in danger, and with them he is able to fly away.

B540.2.p: A helpful horse rescues children from danger.

B541.r: Type 506; BP III 494ff.; Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte 94; Missouri-French: Carrière.
B541.p: An animal rescues a man who is in danger at sea, bringing him safely out of the water.

B541.1.r: (See also B551.)—*Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 868; *Chauvin V 4 No. 2.
B541.1.p: A man escapes from the sea by riding on the back of a fish.

B541.1.1.p: A fish swallows a man to carry him out of the sea and save him from drowning. He escapes by riding on the fish's back.

B541.2.r: Type 506; BP III 494ff.;—N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 405ff. (Passamaquoddy, Shuswap).
B541.2.p: A fox saves a man who is in danger at sea.

B541.3.r: (Cf. B542, B450.)—*Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte 94.—N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Thompson CColl II 408.
B541.3.p: A bird saves a man who is in danger at sea.

B541.4.p: A dog saves a man who is drowning.

B541.4.1.r: Eskimo (Bering Strait): Nelson RBAE XVIII 505, (Greenland): Rink 196.
B541.4.1.p: A dog pulls a boat along by a rope or line in order to save a drowning man.

B541.5.p: A fish saves a ship that is in danger at sea.

B542.p: An animal carries a man through the air to safety, away from danger.

B542.1.p: A bird flies with a man, carrying him to safety.

B542.1.1.r: *Type 301; BP II 300 (Gr. No. 91). See all references under B322.1.—Irish myth: Cross; Missouri-French: Carrière; Finnish: Kalevala rune 7; Japanese: Hartland Science 194, Ikeda.—Africa (Kaffir): Theal 47, 127, (Vai): Ellis 242 No. 49.
B542.1.1.p: An eagle carries a man off to safety.

B542.1.2.r: N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 318 n. 151b, Calif. Indian: Gayton and Newman 95.
B542.1.2.p: A bat rescues a man who is high up, lowering him to the ground in a basket made of spider web.

B542.1.3.p: A measuring worm (inchworm) rescues a man who is at a height.

B542.2.r: (Cf. B41.2.)—*Chauvin V 227f. No. 130; Missouri-French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
B542.2.p: A man escapes from danger by riding away on a flying horse.

B542.2.1.p: A man is carried off to fairyland on the back of a griffin, a winged creature.

B543.r: Scotch: Campbell I 1ff. (dog, hawk, otter).—India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 232 No. 34.
B543.p: An animal finds a person who has been kidnapped or stolen away and leads others to them.

B543.0.1.p: An animal helps a man searching for his wife who has vanished, by assisting in the quest.

B543.1.p: A bottlefly (a large fly) finds a woman who has been stolen and carried off into the sky.

B543.2.p: An animal finds goods that have been stolen.

B543.3.r: (Cf. B535.)—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; *Krappe Balor 80ff.
B543.3.p: An animal acting as a nurse rescues a child who has been stolen.

B543.3.1.p: An elephant rescues a girl who has been stolen.

B544.r: *Fb “höj” I 741 b (fox); Missouri-French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 17 No. 8.—Africa (Zulu): Callaway 147, 241 (dog, frog), (Cameroon): Meinhof 88, 102.
B544.p: An animal frees a person who is held captive.

B544.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 180.
B544.1.p: A grateful animal frees its imprisoned master from captivity.

B545.r: *Type 75. See references to B363.—Penzer V 79 n. 2 (mouse); Japanese: Ikeda.
B545.p: Animals free a creature that has been caught in a trap or net.

B545.1.p: A deer caught in a net is freed by a crow, a mouse and a tortoise working together.

B545.2.p: A rat or mouse chews through a net to free a trapped creature.

B546.p: An animal goes out and finds the body of a man who has died.

B784.1.3.p: A person swallows snake semen or an egg while eating watercress, and a snake develops inside.

B784.1.5.p: A swallowed blackbeetle reproduces inside a person's body.

B784.1.7.p: A scaly lizard jumps into a person's mouth.
